articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions, Reporting Requirements
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning the blocking and rejecting of transactions, as well as the associated reporting requirements. This update aims to provide further clarity and guidance to financial institutions and other entities on their obligations under OFAC regulations.

The amendments address various scenarios related to compliance with sanctions programs, emphasizing the importance of accurate and timely reporting of blocked property and rejected transactions. The updated FAQs serve as a critical resource for ensuring adherence to U.S. sanctions policies and mitigating potential enforcement risks.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, General Licenses; Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities and individuals connected to Iran. Concurrently, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended existing Frequently Asked Questions to provide further guidance.

In a significant development, OFAC also removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. These removals indicate a recalibration of sanctions policy concerning these nations, though the specific reasons for the delistings were not immediately detailed.

The issuance of new General Licenses aims to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the respective sanctions programs, facilitating humanitarian aid or other permitted activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations target individuals and entities involved in the theft or misappropriation of American intellectual property.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses are intended to provide carve-outs for certain transactions that may otherwise be prohibited, ensuring that legitimate activities are not unduly impacted by the new sanctions.
The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding American innovation and technology from illicit acquisition and exploitation.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and an updated Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This action aims to refine existing sanctions policies concerning Venezuela.

The amendment provides further clarification on authorized activities or transactions related to Venezuela, potentially impacting certain sectors or individuals. The updated FAQ offers additional guidance for compliance with the Venezuela sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba-Related Entities; Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting entities and individuals linked to Iran and Cuba. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to exert pressure on both regimes.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions. These measures aim to clarify the scope of the sanctions and provide guidance for legitimate transactions.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's continued focus on addressing perceived threats from Iran and Cuba through economic sanctions.

The removal may be a result of a change in circumstances, a successful delisting petition, or a policy adjustment. Further details regarding the specific entity or individual removed were not immediately provided.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations

The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating global illicit drug trade and terrorist financing. Further details on the specific individuals and entities designated were not immediately available.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License

The issuance of this General License suggests a specific carve-out for particular activities or sectors, aiming to mitigate unintended consequences of existing sanctions or facilitate certain permitted engagements with Russia.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 Over Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $11,662,930. This settlement addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The settlement is part of a broader enforcement action that also saw FinCEN assess a $1.2 billion penalty against Bank of America for willful failures in its AML program and suspicious activity reporting, with the OCC concurrently assessing a $750 million civil money penalty for similar deficiencies.
OFAC's action underscores the critical importance for financial institutions to maintain robust compliance programs to prevent sanctions breaches across all applicable regimes.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has assessed a $1.2 billion civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. for its willful failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.

Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) by failing to implement and maintain an adequate Anti-Money Laundering (AML) program, conduct due diligence for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions, and file Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs).

The consent order found critical deficiencies and gaps in the bank's proprietary transaction monitoring system, resulting in missed and delayed detection and reporting of over $5 billion of suspicious activity. FinCEN credited $750 million of the penalty for a concurrent OCC action, meaning Bank of America will pay $450 million directly to FinCEN.

articles.headline: Commerce Department Announces $389 Million in R&D Awards to Strengthen U.S. Energy Semiconductor Supply Chain
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce has announced the signing of four letters of intent to provide up to $389 million in federal research and development (R&D) awards under the CHIPS and Science Act. These incentives are designed to accelerate R&D supporting semiconductors and materials crucial for power control, conversion, and delivery, which are foundational to modernizing the domestic grid and powering critical energy infrastructure.

The awards will support projects aimed at developing and scaling domestic capabilities in high-voltage power semiconductors and advanced energy power modules. This includes up to $175 million for Helion to develop semiconductors for fusion power generation, up to $85 million for Commonwealth Fusion Systems for fusion-related electronics, and up to $73 million for Vertical Semiconductor to advance vertical gallium nitride (GaN) power semiconductors for AI data centers.

Additionally, Sibelco will receive up to $56 million to develop next-generation purification and finishing technologies for ultra-high-purity quartz, a material essential to the semiconductor value chain. These investments aim to reduce reliance on overseas manufacturing, strengthen economic and national security, and support the energy pathways underpinning future U.S. semiconductor leadership.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
